Preliminary evidence from a UK-based randomized clinical trial, known as the RECOVERY trial, indicates that dexamethasone reduced mortality by approximately 33% in COVID-19 patients requiring mechanical ventilation and by 20% in those needing oxygen support. However, no benefit was observed in patients with milder disease, and there were no preventive benefits. 2. Dexamethasone may be used cautiously on a case-by-case basis for severely ill patients who are on mechanical ventilation or oxygen support. 3. In the RECOVERY trial, eligible patients were randomly assigned to different treatment arms. Dexamethasone was administered either orally (as a liquid or tablet) or intravenously at a dose of 6 mg once daily for ten days in one of the treatment arms. Pregnant or breastfeeding women were randomized to receive prednisolone, a milder corticosteroid, at a dose of 40 mg orally. 4. Hydroxychloroquine is currently not recommended for use outside of clinical trials due to its potential toxicity and lack of documented benefits. The U.S. FDA revoked the Emergency Use Authorization (EUA) for hydroxychloroquine and chloroquine on June 15, 2020, as the known potential benefits do not outweigh the risks and toxicity. 5. Not all patients with a positive COVID-19 test require hospital admission. Hospitalization is warranted for patients whose clinical presentation necessitates in-patient management for supportive medical care under appropriate isolation precautions. Some patients with initially mild symptoms may deteriorate during the second week of illness. Decisions regarding in-patient versus out-patient monitoring should be individualized, considering clinical presentation, the patient’s ability to self-monitor, the feasibility of safe home isolation, and the risk of transmission in the home environment. 6. Currently, there are no FDA-approved medications specifically approved for the treatment or prevention of COVID-19. During public health emergencies, the FDA may authorize the use of unapproved drugs or unapproved uses of approved drugs under an Emergency Use Authorization (EUA) when no adequate, approved, and available options exist. The FDA has issued EUAs for certain medications for use in hospitalized COVID-19 patients. Researchers are studying new drugs and repurposing existing approved medications for potential COVID-19 treatments. The FDA has also established the Coronavirus Treatment Acceleration Program (CTAP) to expedite the development of new treatments and is collaborating with the National Institutes of Health, drug manufacturers, and researchers to accelerate the process. 7. Remdesivir is an investigational antiviral drug and is not currently FDA-approved to treat or prevent any diseases, including COVID-19. However, the FDA has allowed its use under an Emergency Use Authorization (EUA) issued on May 1, 2020, for hospitalized patients with severe COVID-19. Under the EUA, healthcare providers and patients are informed about the risks of remdesivir. Final data from clinical trials are still required to determine its safety and efficacy in treating COVID-19. 8. Empirical antibiotics are not routinely recommended for COVID-19 patients unless there is a high likelihood of concurrent bacterial infection, such as community-acquired or hospital-acquired bacterial pneumonia. Decisions to administer antibiotics should consider the probability of bacterial infection, illness severity, and antimicrobial stewardship principles. 9. There are currently no FDA-approved antiviral medications specifically for the treatment or prevention of COVID-19. Clinical management focuses on infection prevention, control measures, and supportive care, including supplemental oxygen and mechanical ventilation when necessary. Numerous clinical trials are ongoing globally to evaluate potential treatments for COVID-19. 10. Ivermectin is not approved for the prevention or treatment of COVID-19. While it has approved uses in humans and animals, it should not be taken for COVID-19 unless prescribed by a healthcare provider and obtained from a legitimate source. Laboratory studies have shown some effects of ivermectin on SARS-CoV-2 in vitro, but further testing is required to determine its potential role in preventing or treating COVID-19. 11. There is no conclusive evidence that NSAIDs, such as ibuprofen or naproxen, worsen the course of COVID-19. Regulatory agencies, including the FDA, European Medicines Agency, WHO, and CDC, are monitoring the situation and reviewing new data as it becomes available. Patients who rely on NSAIDs for chronic conditions should consult their healthcare provider for individualized management. All medications, including NSAIDs, should be used according to product labels and healthcare professional advice. 12. At present, there is no vaccine available to prevent COVID-19. The FDA is collaborating with vaccine developers, researchers, and manufacturers to expedite the development and availability of medical products, including vaccines, antibodies, and drugs, to prevent COVID-19. 13. Convalescent plasma is the liquid component of blood collected from individuals who have recovered from COVID-19. These individuals develop antibodies against the virus, which are proteins that may help fight the infection. Convalescent plasma is being investigated as a potential treatment for COVID-19 because there is no approved treatment for the disease, and preliminary data suggest it might help some patients recover. Further research is needed to determine whether convalescent plasma can shorten illness duration, reduce morbidity, or prevent death associated with COVID-19.
